title: Simon did not want God.
paragraphs: Simon did not want God.
He wanted what God could make people think about him.
That is what makes his story terrifying.
Because if we are honest… many people in church today are closer to Simon the Sorcerer than Simon Peter.
The Book of Acts introduces him with language that already exposes the disease inside his soul:
“But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria…” — Acts 8:9
The Greek word for “sorcery” here is μαγεύων (mageuōn).
It is where we derive the word “magic.”
But this was not harmless entertainment.
In the ancient world, mageia often referred to occult manipulation, hidden spiritual practices, invocation rituals, mystical domination, secret knowledge, and attempts to control invisible powers.
Simon built his identity on spiritual performance.
Not surrender.
And people adored him for it.
Acts 8:10 says:
“To whom they all gave heed, from the least to the greatest, saying, This man is the great power of God.”
The phrase “great power” in Greek is:

ἡ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ καλουμένη μεγάλη
(hē dynamis tou theou hē kaloumenē megalē)
Literally:
“The Power of God called Great.”
Imagine hearing crowds whisper your name like that every day.
Imagine becoming addicted to being spiritually impressive.
Imagine confusing influence with intimacy with God.
That was Simon.
And honestly…
that is still happening now.
Some people do not want Jesus.

They want the platform.
The attention.
The authority.
The reactions.
The mystery.
The appearance of anointing.
The feeling of importance.
They want people amazed by them.
Simon’s entire identity depended on being seen as spiritually extraordinary.
Then Philip arrived.
Not with manipulation.
Not with theatrics.
Not with occult mystery.
But with the Gospel.
Acts 8:12 says:
“But when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized…”
Something terrifying happened to Simon that day.
For the first time in his life…
he encountered a power he could not manufacture.
Demons leave when magicians perform tricks.
But demons scream when Jesus arrives.
And Simon noticed the difference.
This is why the text becomes psychologically fascinating.
Acts 8:13 says:
“Then Simon himself believed also…”
At first glance, this sounds beautiful.
But the deeper context becomes unsettling.
Because Scripture immediately says:
“…and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip, and wondered, beholding the miracles and signs which were done.”
The Greek word for “wondered” is:
ἐξίστατο (existato)

It means:
astonished,
overwhelmed,
mentally shaken.
But notice carefully:
The text never says Simon was overwhelmed by repentance.
He was overwhelmed by power.
That distinction matters.
A lot.
There are people emotional in church services who are still unconverted.
People cry over atmosphere while never surrendering their sin.
People can admire spiritual power while secretly remaining in rebellion against God.
Simon followed the miracles.
Not the cross.
Then came the moment that exposed everything hidden inside him.
Peter and John arrived in Samaria.
Believers began receiving the Holy Spirit.
Acts 8:18 says:
“And when Simon saw that through laying on of the apostles’ hands the Holy Ghost was given…”
Stop there.
“When Simon SAW.”
That word matters.
Simon was still viewing spirituality through the lens of visible power and control.
He was still thinking like a sorcerer.
Because sorcery is obsessed with control.
The Kingdom of God is about surrender.

Sorcery says:
“How can I harness spiritual power?”

The Gospel says:
“How can I die to myself?”
And Simon could not understand the difference.
Then he committed one of the darkest spiritual moments in the New Testament.
Acts 8:19:
“Saying, Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost.”
He tried to buy the Holy Spirit.
Imagine that.

The Creator of heaven and earth…
reduced to a transaction.
The Greek word Simon uses for “power” is ἐξουσία (exousia).

Authority.
Influence.
Delegated dominion.
He wanted apostolic authority without apostolic death.
He wanted manifestation without sanctification.
He wanted influence without repentance.
He wanted spiritual appearance without inner transformation.
And Peter exploded.
Acts 8:20:
“But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.”
The Greek phrase is devastating:

τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ
(tēn dōrean tou theou)
“The free gift of God.”
FREE.
Simon understood prices.
But he did not understand grace.
That is the tragedy.

Religion says:
“What must I pay?”

Jesus says:
“It is finished.”
And then Peter says something so severe that most modern churches would never dare say it out loud.
Acts 8:21:
“Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God.”
The Greek word for “right” is:
εὐθεῖα (eutheia)

Straight.
Aligned.
True.
Simon’s heart was crooked.
And heaven saw it.
You can fool crowds.
You can fool social media.
You can fool church people.

You can quote Scripture.
Raise hands in worship.
Carry a microphone.
Lead Bible studies.
Talk about revival.
And still have a crooked heart before God.
That should terrify all of us.
Then Peter reveals the real condition of Simon’s soul.
Acts 8:23:
“For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.”
“Gall” in Greek is:

χολὴν πικρίας
(cholēn pikrias)
Poison bitterness.
Not woundedness.
Poison.
Simon’s obsession with power came from inner corruption.
Because many people seek power when they are empty inside.
They crave control because they are spiritually broken.
They crave admiration because they are starving for identity.
They crave influence because they are terrified of insignificance.
Simon did not merely want power.
He wanted to become untouchable.
And the Gospel destroys that illusion.
Jesus does not come to make us impressive.
He comes to crucify us.
That is why Simon’s story still convicts the modern church.
Because celebrity Christianity has made spiritual fame look holy.

Followers.
Views.
Platforms.
Influence.
Crowds.
Meanwhile Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself…” — Matthew 16:24
The Greek phrase for “deny himself” is:

ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν
(aparnēsasthō heauton)
Disown yourself.
Not promote yourself.
Disown yourself.
Simon wanted spiritual authority that would elevate him.
Jesus offers a cross that kills pride.
And that is where many walk away.
Because everybody wants resurrection power.
Few want crucifixion.
Be honest.
This exposed something deeper than you expected.

How many prayers were really about surrender…
and how many were secretly about control?

How much “ministry” was really love for Jesus…
and how much was desire for recognition?
How much exhaustion comes from trying to appear spiritually strong while secretly feeling spiritually hollow?
Simon’s story survives in Scripture because God wanted future generations to see this warning clearly:

You can stand near the move of God…
and still completely misunderstand God Himself.
Judas kissed Jesus and betrayed Him.
Simon witnessed miracles and still desired power more than purity.
Proximity is not transformation.
And yet…
there is still mercy hidden inside this story.
Peter tells Simon in Acts 8:22:
“Repent therefore of this thy wickedness, and pray God, if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee.”
The Greek word for repent is:
μετανόησον (metanoēson)

Change your mind.
Turn completely.
Abandon the old path.
Even Simon was invited to repent.

That means there is hope for proud hearts.
Hope for performative Christianity.
Hope for hidden motives.
Hope for spiritual hypocrisy.
Hope for those addicted to appearance.
Jesus still saves people who wanted the wrong things.
But only if they finally surrender.
Not perform.
Not pretend.
Surrender.
Somebody reading this has been exhausted trying to look spiritually powerful while secretly battling emptiness.
Jesus never asked you to become impressive.
He asked you to follow Him.
That is different.
Very different.
And maybe the reason your soul still feels restless is because platforms cannot heal what only repentance can.
Maybe you chased spiritual influence while neglecting intimacy with God.
Maybe you wanted gifts more than holiness.
Maybe you wanted people to notice you more than you wanted God to transform you.
Simon’s story is not just history.
It is a mirror.

Some people wanted the power of God so badly…
they never realized they were resisting the presence of God Himself.
